title: Evaluating policy pathways to end plastic pollution
gist: An Oxford Economics study commissioned by the chemical industry's ICCA finds that waste-collection, recycling and circularity policies cut plastic leakage as much as an upstream cap on virgin plastics production, but at substantially lower economic cost and with greater recycling gains.

insights.claim: Policies that strengthen waste collection, recycling, and circularity (including trade in recyclable waste) can achieve the same reduction in plastic leakage into the environment as an upstream cap on virgin plastics production.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Investors and companies exposed to virgin-plastics/petrochemical production should note that downstream waste-management policy is being positioned by industry-funded research as an equally effective, less disruptive alternative to production caps.
insights.quote: policies focused on improving waste collection, recycling, and circularity can achieve the same reduction in plastic leakage as an upstream cap on virgin plastics production

insights.claim: Waste-management-focused policy packages deliver significantly greater recycling gains than an upstream cap on virgin plastics production, for the same reduction in plastic leakage.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Suggests recycling/circularity infrastructure investment could be favored by future plastics regulation over blunt production limits, a relevant signal for chemicals and waste-management sector positioning.
insights.quote: delivering significantly greater recycling gains and substantially lower economic costs

insights.claim: An upstream cap on virgin plastics production imposes substantially higher economic costs than policy packages targeting waste collection, recycling, and circularity, for an equivalent reduction in plastic leakage.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Chemical and plastics producers facing potential production-cap regulation (e.g. under a global plastics treaty) can point to this finding to argue for waste-focused alternatives with lower compliance cost.
insights.locator: The analysis finds that policies focused on improving waste collection

insights.claim: Policymakers should target the direct drivers of mismanaged plastic waste (collection, recycling, circularity, recyclable-waste trade) rather than relying primarily on broad restrictions on plastics production to curb plastic pollution.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: A framework investors can use to gauge which regulatory approach (production caps vs. waste-system investment) is more likely to gain traction in plastics-treaty negotiations, informing sector risk assessment for chemicals/petrochemicals vs. waste-management and recycling companies.
insights.quote: highlight the importance of targeting the drivers of mismanaged waste directly, rather than relying primarily on broad restrictions on plastics production

insights.claim: The report was commissioned by the International Council of Chemical Associations (ICCA), a global trade association representing chemical (and by extension plastics-producing) companies, meaning its conclusion favoring waste-management policy over production caps comes from industry-funded research.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Investors should weight the study's pro-recycling, anti-production-cap conclusion against the sponsor's commercial interest in avoiding upstream production restrictions before treating it as a neutral policy signal.
insights.quote: A study for The International Council of Chemical Associations (ICCA)
insights.locator: Evaluating policy pathways to end plastic pollution

insights.claim: Oxford Economics used a structural economic model to compare an upstream virgin-plastics production cap against waste-management policy packages, supplemented by lessons drawn from past multilateral environmental agreements to inform treaty design.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Signals that global plastics-treaty negotiators are being presented with formal economic-cost modeling alongside historical treaty precedent, which could shape the design of the pending global plastics agreement.
insights.quote: Using a structural economic model, we compare an upstream cap on virgin plastics production with policy packages that strengthen waste collection, recycling, and circularity

insights.claim: This report follows on from ICCA's earlier Oxford Economics report, 'Mapping the Plastics Value Chain,' shifting the research agenda from descriptive value-chain analysis to active evaluation of specific policy interventions ahead of plastics-treaty decisions.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Indicates an ongoing, sequenced industry research/advocacy campaign around plastics policy, worth tracking for further ICCA-commissioned releases that could influence treaty terms.
insights.quote: Building on ICCA’s earlier report, Mapping the Plastics Value Chain, this study moves from describing how plastics flow through the global economy to evaluating the consequences of different policy interventions.
